reference.source: Standard endocrinology texts and adrenal insufficiency guidance
clinicalPearls: An inherited, usually autosomal recessive, cause of isolated cortisol deficiency with characteristically preserved mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) production
Commonly caused by mutations in MC2R (the ACTH receptor) or MRAP (its accessory protein), which impair the adrenal response to ACTH
Presents in infancy or childhood with hypoglycaemia, prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, recurrent infections, or collapse during illness
Marked skin hyperpigmentation reflects the very high ACTH levels driven by absent cortisol feedback
Because aldosterone is intact, the salt-wasting, hyperkalaemia, and hyponatraemia typical of other primary adrenal failure are usually absent
Tall stature relative to family is a recognised and somewhat paradoxical feature in some genetic subtypes
Treatment is glucocorticoid replacement, with careful sick-day dosing to prevent adrenal crisis; mineralocorticoid replacement is generally not required
reference.pathophysiology: Familial glucocorticoid deficiency results from failure of the adrenal cortex to respond to ACTH. Mutations in MC2R disable the melanocortin-2 receptor through which ACTH stimulates cortisol synthesis, and mutations in MRAP prevent that receptor from being trafficked to the cell surface; other subtypes affect antioxidant defence or replication pathways in the adrenal. Cortisol production in the zona fasciculata fails while the renin-angiotensin-driven zona glomerulosa continues to make aldosterone. Loss of cortisol feedback drives ACTH to very high levels, causing hyperpigmentation, and leaves the child vulnerable to hypoglycaemia and life-threatening crisis during stress.
additionalDifferentials: Adrenoleukodystrophy and other metabolic adrenal disease
additionalInvestigations: Paired serum cortisol and plasma ACTH, showing low cortisol with markedly elevated ACTH
Short synacthen (ACTH stimulation) test demonstrating an absent cortisol response
Electrolytes and plasma renin/aldosterone to confirm preserved mineralocorticoid function
Blood glucose during illness or symptoms
Genetic testing of MC2R, MRAP, and related genes
Very-long-chain fatty acids and adrenal antibodies to exclude mimics
redFlags: Hypoglycaemia, seizures, or collapse indicating adrenal crisis
Intercurrent illness without stress-dose glucocorticoid cover
Failure to recognise deepening hyperpigmentation as a sign of severe glucocorticoid deficiency
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, reliable glucocorticoid replacement, and education about sick-day rules and emergency treatment, prognosis is good; the principal danger is unrecognised adrenal crisis, particularly hypoglycaemia in infancy, which can be fatal or cause neurological injury.
pitfalls: Expecting salt-wasting and electrolyte disturbance and therefore discounting adrenal insufficiency when they are absent
Missing the diagnosis in a hypoglycaemic or persistently jaundiced neonate
Failing to provide stress-dose cover and an emergency plan
references: Endocrine society guidance on adrenal insufficiency
management: Glucocorticoid replacement with hydrocortisone as the definitive therapy for the isolated cortisol deficiency
Mineralocorticoid replacement is generally not required, as aldosterone production is preserved
Structured sick-day rules with stress-dose glucocorticoid, and parenteral hydrocortisone plus intravenous glucose for adrenal crisis and hypoglycaemia
Provision of an emergency hydrocortisone injection kit and medical-alert identification with caregiver training
Monitoring of growth, hyperpigmentation and adequacy of replacement to avoid over- or under-treatment
Genetic counselling with MC2R and MRAP testing and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
Paediatric endocrinology follow-up, with early diagnosis to prevent hypoglycaemic neurological injury
